item.content:encoded:
The University of Strathclyde is inviting applications for a postgraduate research opportunity exploring the history of unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948. The three-year PhD research project offers an opportunity for a prospective doctoral researcher to investigate alternative approaches to health, grassroots activism, community organising and the experiences of people who participated in health movements outside mainstream medical practices.

The project is particularly relevant to applicants interested in history, healthcare history, public health, social movements, complementary and alternative medicine, health policy, medical humanities, community activism, oral history, and the social history of medicine.

The successful applicant will undertake independent doctoral research while working with academic supervisors in the University of Strathclyde’s History subject area. The research will also be affiliated with a wider Wellcome-funded research project examining the transnational history of AIDS denial.

The studentship provides Home fees and a stipend for three years, with study expected to commence on 1 January 2027.

Opportunity Overview

The University of Strathclyde’s PhD project, titled “Unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948,” seeks to develop a deeper historical understanding of alternative and unconventional approaches to health in Britain from the establishment of the National Health Service in 1948 through the late 20th and early 21st centuries.

The research recognises that health activism outside mainstream medicine has played an important role in British society for decades. Although alternative health movements became particularly visible during the COVID-19 pandemic, debates around alternative medicine, health autonomy, medical authority, patient rights, and community-based approaches to well-being have a much longer history.

The project therefore provides an opportunity to investigate how individuals and communities engaged with unconventional approaches to health, why they became involved, how these movements shaped everyday experiences of health, and how governments, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and public health practitioners responded.

Key Details of the PhD Studentship

  • University: University of Strathclyde
  • Faculty: Humanities and Social Sciences
  • Subject: History
  • Programme: PhD History
  • Research project: Unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948
  • Study mode: Full-time
  • Duration: 3 years
  • Number of places: 1
  • Opening date: 30 July 2026
  • Application deadline: 30 October 2026 at 5:00 PM BST
  • Expected start date: 1 January 2027
  • Funding: Home tuition fees plus stipend
  • Stipend for January 2027 starters: £16,354, based on the pro-rata equivalent of £21,805
  • Monthly stipend: Approximately £1,817
  • Stipend: Tax-free and paid monthly
  • Supervisors: Dr Hannah Elizabeth and Professor Matthew Smith

About the Research Project

The research project examines the history of health movements that challenged or operated outside conventional medical approaches in Britain.

Since the founding of the NHS in 1948, various grassroots organisations, activists, and communities have questioned established approaches to medicine and healthcare. These movements have included campaigns around alternative medicine, patient autonomy, mental health reform, nutrition, community healthcare, and other forms of health activism.

The PhD will investigate these developments historically, asking not only what these movements believed but also what it meant to participate in them.

Among the central questions the project seeks to explore are the following:

  • What was it like to participate in unorthodox health movements?
  • How did individuals become involved in alternative health communities?
  • What motivated people to challenge mainstream medical practices?
  • How did membership of health movements affect people’s everyday experiences of health?
  • How did health activists organise within local communities?
  • What role did media representations play in shaping perceptions of alternative health?
  • How did public health practitioners respond to these movements?
  • How did healthcare workers and policymakers respond to challenges from health activists?
  • How did alternative health movements evolve from the post-war period to the present?
  • What impact did these movements have on broader understandings of health and medicine?

These questions make the studentship particularly suitable for researchers who want to examine health not simply as a medical issue but as a social, cultural, political, and historical phenomenon.

Suggested Research Areas

Although applicants are encouraged to develop their own research programme, the University has identified several possible areas of focus.

1. The History of the British Anti-Vaccination Movement

One possible area is the historical development of the anti-vaccination movement in Britain during the late 20th century and beyond.

A project in this area could examine how opposition to vaccination developed, how activists organised themselves, the arguments they presented, the communities they built, and the ways in which government and public health institutions responded.

The research could also examine how historical anti-vaccination activism influenced later debates around vaccination and public health.

2. Cancer Denial

Another potential research area is the history of cancer denial.

This could involve investigating individuals or communities that rejected conventional understandings of cancer, questioned established cancer treatments or promoted alternative explanations and treatments.

Such research could examine the relationship between medical authority, patient experiences, alternative health beliefs and public communication.

3. Complementary and Alternative Medicine

The project also welcomes research into Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) and its relationship with everyday health.

Researchers could examine the development and popularity of practices such as herbal medicine, homeopathy, naturopathy, and other forms of complementary healthcare.

A project could investigate why people turned to these approaches, how practitioners developed their communities, and how CAM interacted with the NHS and conventional healthcare.

4. Media Representations of Alternative Health Movements

Media and communications provide another potentially important area of study.

A PhD could explore how newspapers, television, radio, magazines, digital media, and other communication channels represented alternative health movements.

This could include examining whether media coverage contributed to the growth of particular movements, reinforced public concerns, or shaped perceptions of alternative healthcare.

5. Regional Unorthodox Health Activism

Applicants may also consider focusing on health activism in particular regions of Britain.

A regional study could reveal how local histories, communities, social conditions, and healthcare provisions influenced the development of alternative health movements.

This approach could be especially valuable for understanding how national debates around health translated into local activism.

6. Spiritual and Religious Health Communities

Another potential research direction is the relationship between health activism and spiritual or religious communities.

This could examine communities that developed alternative understandings of health and well-being based on spiritual, religious, or philosophical beliefs.

Researchers could explore how these communities organised, how members understood health and illness, and how their practices interacted with mainstream medical institutions.

7. The History of Wellness Movements

The project also provides an opportunity to study the emergence and development of modern “wellness” movements.

A research project could investigate how ideas about well-being, lifestyle, nutrition, fitness, self-care, and personal responsibility evolved over time.

It could also explore the historical relationship between wellness culture and broader changes in healthcare, consumer culture, media, and society.

Connection to a Wider Wellcome-Funded Research Project

The studentship will be affiliated with the Wellcome-funded project “A Transnational History of AIDS Denial: Origins, Manifestations, and Persistence, 1981 to the present.”

This connection creates an opportunity for the doctoral researcher to situate their work within a wider scholarly investigation into unconventional approaches to health and medicine.

Applicants whose proposed research examines similar forms of unorthodox health activity during the 20th and/or 21st centuries are particularly encouraged to apply.

The relationship between the studentship and the wider project may also provide a valuable intellectual environment for exploring questions concerning health beliefs, medical authority, activism, public communication, and historical change.

Funding and Financial Support

One of the major attractions of this PhD opportunity is the financial support attached to the studentship.

The award covers Home tuition fees and provides a stipend for the duration of the three-year programme.

For candidates commencing study on 1 January 2027, the stated stipend is £16,354, described by the University as the pro-rata equivalent of the £21,805 rate.

The stipend is expected to be paid in monthly installments of approximately £1,817 and is tax-free.

The stipend is also likely to increase each year, subject to the applicable funding arrangements.

The funding is intended to support the successful doctoral researcher throughout the three-year period of study, provided the programme is completed within the funded duration.

Applicants should carefully review the University’s funding conditions and fee arrangements before applying, particularly where international fee differences may apply.

Academic Supervision

The successful doctoral researcher will be supervised by academics in the University of Strathclyde’s History subject area.

The listed supervisory team includes:

Dr Hannah Elizabeth
Research Fellow, History

Professor Matthew Smith
Professor, History

Applicants are required to contact the supervisory team before submitting their formal application.

This preliminary discussion is an important part of the application process because applicants need to ensure that their proposed research aligns with the themes and objectives of the studentship.

Application Process

Applicants must complete two important stages.

Step 1: Contact the Supervisory Team

Before submitting the formal application, applicants should contact one of the following:

  • Dr Hannah Elizabeth at hannah.elizabeth@strath.ac.uk
  • Professor Matt Smith at m.smith@strath.ac.uk

Applicants should introduce their proposed research ideas and discuss how their project relates to the themes of the studentship.

This stage is important because the University wants applicants to demonstrate that their research proposal is compatible with the project’s focus before submitting the formal application.

Step 2: Submit the Formal PhD Application

After engaging with the supervisory team, applicants should submit an online application through the University’s Pegasus application system for PhD History.

The application should specify the start date of 1 January 2027.

In the funding section of the application form, applicants should enter the project title:

“Unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948.”

Required Application Documents

Applicants must prepare a complete application containing all required supporting documents.

1. 1,000-Word Research Proposal

The research proposal should be approximately 1,000 words and explain the research the applicant intends to undertake over the three years of the PhD.

Applicants may propose either:

  • one central research project; or
  • several closely related case studies.

The proposal should demonstrate a clear understanding of the historical subject, establish the research questions, and explain the proposed approach to investigating unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948.

Applicants should also ensure they have completed the first application step and contacted the supervisory team before submitting the proposal.

2. 500-Word Personal Statement

Applicants must submit a 500-word personal statement explaining why they want to undertake the studentship.

The statement should provide a clear explanation of the applicant’s academic motivation and interest in the proposed area of research.

It should also demonstrate why the applicant is well suited to doctoral research in this field.

3. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a CV of up to three pages.

The CV should clearly present relevant academic qualifications, research experience, publications where applicable, professional experience, and other achievements relevant to doctoral study.

4. Two Academic References

Applicants must provide two academic references.

The references should include the referees’ names and full contact details.

5. Degree Certificates and Transcripts

Applicants must provide copies of all degree certificates and academic transcripts obtained to date.

These documents should allow the University to assess the applicant’s academic background and eligibility.

6. English Language Evidence

Where English is not the applicant’s first language, the application should include evidence of English-language proficiency.

The University specifies IELTS Academic, taken within the two years preceding commencement of study, or an equivalent accepted English-language qualification.

Applicants should ensure that their language evidence meets the University’s requirements.

APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications is:

30 October 2026 at 5:00 PM BST

Applicants are strongly advised not to wait until the final hours to submit their applications.

Because the University states that incomplete applications will not be considered, applicants should allow sufficient time to upload every required document and verify that their application is complete.

Important Warning About Generative AI

The University of Strathclyde explicitly addresses the use of generative artificial intelligence in its application guidance.

Applicants are advised that their research proposals should be written in their own words.

The University notes that generative AI tools can produce inaccurate or outdated information and that academics may be able to identify text generated using such tools.

For a doctoral application, this is particularly important because the research proposal is intended to demonstrate the applicant’s own academic ability, research skills, critical thinking, and capacity to develop a viable PhD project.

Applicants should therefore use appropriate academic research practices and ensure that their proposal genuinely represents their own thinking, research interests, and academic writing abilities.

Selection and Interview Process

After the application deadline, applications will be reviewed and ranked by a selection panel.

Only complete applications will be considered.

Applicants who are shortlisted for an interview are expected to be notified in early to mid-November 2026.

Interviews will take place online during the week beginning 23 November 2026.

An important feature of the process is that interview questions will be provided to shortlisted candidates in advance.

This gives shortlisted applicants an opportunity to prepare carefully for the interview and reflect on their proposed research, academic background, and motivation for pursuing the PhD.

The successful applicant must be able to begin their doctoral studies on 1 January 2027.

How to Develop a Strong Application

Competition for funded doctoral studentships can be significant, so applicants should approach the application strategically.

Develop a Focused Research Question

Rather than attempting to investigate every form of alternative health activism in Britain, applicants should develop a manageable research focus.

A strong proposal should establish a clear historical problem and explain why that problem deserves further research.

Demonstrate Historical Significance

Applicants should explain why their proposed topic matters historically.

For example, a proposal could examine how alternative health movements changed relationships between patients and medical professionals, contributed to debates about healthcare policy or influenced public understandings of health.

Connect the Research to the Studentship Themes

The proposed project should clearly relate to unorthodox approaches to health, activism, community organisation or alternative medical practices.

Applicants should demonstrate that they understand the purpose of the studentship rather than submitting a generic history research proposal.

Consider Primary Sources

Because the project encourages archival research and oral history, applicants should think carefully about the types of primary sources that could support their research.

Potential sources could include archival records, newspapers, campaign materials, organisational documents, personal accounts, oral histories, media coverage, and other historical records.

The specific sources will depend on the proposed research question.

Demonstrate Originality

A competitive PhD proposal should go beyond simply describing an existing movement.

Applicants should identify an aspect of the topic that could contribute something new to historical scholarship.

The research proposal should therefore demonstrate curiosity, analytical thinking, and a clear understanding of the potential contribution of the research.

Contact the Supervisors Early

Applicants should not overlook the requirement to contact the supervisory team before submitting the formal application.

Early communication can help applicants refine their research ideas and ensure that their proposed project fits the available supervision and wider research themes.

Why This PhD Opportunity Is Significant

The project provides an opportunity to study the relationship between medicine, society, activism, and individual experiences of health.

Unorthodox health movements can reveal important historical questions about trust in medical institutions, patient autonomy, public health communication, healthcare inequality, and the ways people seek information and support outside conventional systems.

The project is also particularly timely because debates around alternative medicine, vaccination, wellness, medical authority, and health information have become increasingly prominent in contemporary society.

By placing these debates within a longer historical context, doctoral research can help explain where these movements came from, how they developed, and why they continue to influence discussions about health.

Potential Career and Academic Benefits

A three-year PhD at the University of Strathclyde can provide extensive research and academic development.

The successful researcher will have the opportunity to develop skills in areas such as the following:

  • Historical research
  • Archival research
  • Oral history
  • Qualitative research
  • Critical analysis
  • Academic writing
  • Research design
  • Interview techniques
  • Analysis of social movements
  • Health and medical history
  • Public health history
  • Historical interpretation
  • Presentation of research findings
  • Independent project management

These skills can be valuable for careers in academia, research, museums and archives, public policy, heritage, healthcare research, public history, communications, education, and other research-intensive sectors.

Visit HERE for more information about the University of Strathclyde Unorthodox Health Activism in Britain After 1948 PhD Studentship 2027 opportunity.

Important Dates

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

  • 30 July 2026: Applications open
  • 30 October 2026 at 5:00 PM BST: Application deadline
  • Early to mid-November 2026: Shortlisted applicants expected to be notified
  • Week beginning 23 November 2026: Online interviews
  • 1 January 2027: Expected commencement of the PhD

Final Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should make sure they have completed every required stage.

  • Contact the supervisory team with research proposal ideas.
  • Confirm that the proposed project aligns with the studentship themes.
  • Prepare a 1,000-word research proposal.
  • Prepare a 500-word personal statement.
  • Prepare a CV of no more than three pages.
  • Arrange two academic references with full contact details.
  • Upload all degree certificates and academic transcripts.
  • Provide IELTS Academic or an accepted equivalent where required.
  • Select PhD History through the University’s online application system.
  • Select the start date of 1 January 2027.
  • Enter “Unorthodox health activism in Britain after 1948” in the funding section.
  • Check that every required document has been uploaded.
  • Submit the complete application before 5:00 PM BST on 30 October 2026.

Conclusion

The University of Strathclyde Unorthodox Health Activism in Britain after 1948 PhD Studentship 2027 presents a distinctive opportunity for doctoral researchers interested in the history of medicine, health activism, alternative healthcare, and grassroots movements in Britain.

The project goes beyond conventional medical history by examining the experiences of individuals and communities that challenged established approaches to healthcare. Through archival research and oral history, the successful researcher will have the opportunity to investigate how alternative health movements emerged, how people became involved in them and how these movements influenced everyday experiences of health and interactions with medical institutions.

With three years of funding, Home tuition fees, and a tax-free stipend, the studentship offers substantial financial support for doctoral study. The connection to a wider Wellcome-funded research project also provides an important research context for investigating unconventional approaches to health during the 20th and 21st centuries.

Prospective applicants should begin preparing early, particularly because they are required to contact the supervisory team before submitting their formal application. A carefully developed research proposal, a strong academic record, complete supporting documentation, and a clear explanation of the project’s historical significance will be important components of a competitive application.

The application deadline is 30 October 2026 at 5:00 PM BST, and the successful candidate is expected to commence the PhD on 1 January 2027.

The University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship 2026 provides substantial financial support for high-achieving students undertaking doctoral research at the University of Waikato in New Zealand. Open to eligible domestic and international students, the scholarship offers a living allowance of up to NZ$33,000 per year for as long as 36 months, together with domestic doctoral tuition fees and the University’s Student Services Fee.

Established in 1996 to promote excellence in postgraduate research, the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship supports candidates who have demonstrated strong academic achievement, research readiness and the potential to make a meaningful contribution through advanced research. The number of scholarships awarded each year is not fixed and depends on the funding available.

The scholarship covers a wide range of research areas, including arts, business and management, computer science, mathematics, education, health, engineering, law, Māori and Indigenous studies, science, social sciences and environmental studies.

Applications are considered in four scholarship rounds each year. The official closing dates are 31 January, 30 April, 31 July and 31 October. As of August 2026, the next application deadline is therefore 31 October 2026.

About the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship

The University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship was established to provide financial assistance to outstanding candidates who have received an Offer of Place for an approved higher research degree at the University.

The scholarship is not simply awarded on the basis of admission to a doctoral programme. Candidates must separately demonstrate strong academic credentials, readiness to undertake independent research and the potential for their proposed research to generate meaningful academic or wider societal impact.

The University considers applications in four competitive rounds each year rather than continuously awarding scholarships as applications arrive.

Selection panels normally meet in:

  • Early March
  • Early June
  • Early September
  • Early December

Applications are not considered outside these scheduled rounds.

Scholarship Value

The standard University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship provides a substantial package of financial support.

Successful recipients may receive:

  • NZ$33,000 living allowance per year
  • Monthly stipend payments
  • Funding for up to 36 months
  • Domestic tuition fees for the eligible doctoral programme
  • University Student Services Fee

The standard living allowance totals NZ$33,000 for every 12 months and is normally paid in monthly instalments for up to three years.

For approved part-time students, the living allowance is paid on a proportional basis.

The Scholarships Executive may also offer a fees-only scholarship in some circumstances. A fees-only award normally covers domestic tuition fees and the Student Services Fee but does not include the NZ$33,000 annual living allowance.

Costs Not Covered by the Scholarship

Applicants should be aware that the scholarship does not necessarily cover every expense associated with studying in New Zealand.

Recipients are responsible for finding other sources of funding for additional costs such as:

  • Medical or health insurance
  • Relocation and moving expenses
  • Research-related expenses not otherwise funded
  • Personal living costs exceeding the stipend
  • Other miscellaneous expenses

The official regulations explicitly state that medical insurance, moving costs and research expenses must be met through other means.

International applicants should therefore prepare a realistic financial plan rather than assuming the scholarship eliminates all costs associated with doctoral study.

Duration of the Scholarship

The maximum scholarship tenure is:

36 months, or three years, of full-time doctoral enrolment.

Part-time arrangements may extend the calendar duration of the scholarship, but the value and duration are adjusted proportionally.

For candidates entering the Doctor of Health Science, Doctor of Musical Arts or Doctor of Juridical Science, scholarship tenure begins when the student commences Part 1 of the relevant doctoral programme.

If the recipient submits their thesis, withdraws from the doctoral programme or otherwise ends their doctoral enrolment before the end of the scholarship period, scholarship payments also end.

Who Can Apply?

The scholarship is available to a broad range of applicants, including New Zealand and international students.

According to the 2026 scholarship regulations, eligible applicants may include:

  • New Zealand citizens
  • New Zealand permanent residents
  • New Zealand Resident Class Visa holders
  • Australian citizens or permanent residents domiciled in New Zealand
  • International students

This means the scholarship is genuinely available to qualified candidates from outside New Zealand.

However, nationality alone does not determine eligibility. Applicants must satisfy several important academic and procedural requirements.

Eligible Doctoral Programmes

Applicants must hold an Offer of Place in an eligible doctoral qualification at the University of Waikato.

The scholarship regulations specifically identify:

  • Doctor of Philosophy
  • Doctor of Health Science
  • Doctor of Musical Arts
  • Doctor of Juridical Science

Applicants must not have commenced enrolment in the eligible degree before the closing date of the scholarship round in which they are being considered, subject to the detailed timing provisions in the regulations.

Important Note for Doctor of Education Applicants

Although the University offers the Doctor of Education, the principal University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship regulations treat EdD candidates differently.

The regulations note that candidates enrolling in an EdD may instead apply for the University of Waikato Taught Postgraduate Scholarship for Part 1 and the Doctoral Catalyst Scholarship for Part 2.

Applicants interested specifically in the EdD should therefore check the appropriate funding route rather than assuming they qualify for the standard Doctoral Scholarship described here.

Academic Requirements

Admission to higher research degree study generally requires a strong academic foundation.

Prospective candidates would normally be expected to have completed:

  • A Bachelor’s degree with Honours, or
  • A Master’s degree

The qualifying degree must include a significant research component.

According to the University’s doctoral admissions process, the research component normally needs to consist of a thesis, dissertation or research project representing at least 25% of one year of the qualifying degree.

Research-methods courses alone do not count as the required research component.

Applicants must also normally have achieved at least a Second Class, First Division result in the qualification used for doctoral admission.

Scholarship Academic Standard

The scholarship itself is more competitive than simply meeting the minimum doctoral admission requirements.

The 2026 regulations specify that candidates normally require a minimum:

GPA of A-

calculated from the qualification being used for entry to the doctoral programme.

Having an A- GPA does not guarantee a scholarship. It establishes the minimum academic threshold within the scholarship selection framework.

Additional Selection Criteria

The University considers more than grades.

Other factors can include:

  • Previous research experience
  • Professional experience relevant to the proposed research
  • Readiness to undertake independent research
  • Academic references
  • Research publications
  • Capacity of the supervisory panel to support the project
  • Alignment with University, Faculty, School or Research Institute priorities
  • Understanding of Mātauranga Māori and Pacific knowledges where relevant
  • Potential contribution to sustainable development
  • Wider impact of the proposed research

The regulations specifically note that selection may consider alignment with institutional research priorities and the potential for research to generate impact, including advancement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

Who Is Not Eligible?

Applicants are considered ineligible if they:

  • Already hold a doctoral degree or equivalent qualification
  • Do not have an Offer of Place by the relevant scholarship-round deadline
  • Have already been considered twice for the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship

Candidates who have not yet obtained an Offer of Place when a round closes may apply again in a subsequent round if they continue to meet all other requirements.

Candidates are therefore allowed a maximum of two scholarship selection attempts. If unsuccessful in their first round, they may apply once more.

Step 1: Check Your Eligibility for Doctoral Study

Before thinking about the scholarship itself, candidates should determine whether they meet the academic requirements for their chosen University of Waikato research degree.

The University offers higher research qualifications including:

  • Doctor of Philosophy
  • Doctor of Health Science
  • Doctor of Education
  • Doctor of Musical Arts
  • Doctor of Juridical Science
  • Master of Philosophy

Applicants should carefully review the regulations for the specific programme they are considering because individual research degrees may have additional requirements.

International candidates must also satisfy the University’s applicable English-language requirements.

Step 2: Find a University of Waikato Supervisor

A major feature of the University of Waikato doctoral application process is that applicants must identify an appropriate supervisor before submitting the formal application.

Prospective students should explore University staff profiles and identify researchers whose interests align with the proposed doctoral topic.

Potential supervisors can be searched according to factors such as:

  • Research interests
  • Publications
  • Previous doctoral supervision
  • Availability to supervise
  • Current projects

Applicants should then contact appropriate academics directly to discuss the proposed research and its alignment with the supervisor’s expertise.

Step 3: Obtain an Invitation to Apply

A prospective supervisor must formally agree to supervise the candidate before the doctoral application can progress.

Once agreement has been reached, the University of Waikato supervisor will provide the prospective applicant with an:

Invitation to Apply

This step is essential.

Candidates who do not possess an Invitation to Apply will not have their doctoral application considered.

Applicants should therefore avoid approaching the doctoral admissions process as though they can simply submit an online form first and look for a supervisor afterward.

Step 4: Prepare Your Application Documents

After receiving the Invitation to Apply, candidates should prepare all documentation required for the Application to Enrol.

Applicants need to identify at least one University of Waikato supervisor who has agreed to supervise them.

They must also provide contact information for:

Two academic referees

who are willing to be contacted as part of the doctoral admissions process.

Candidates should carefully check the University’s PhD and Higher Research Degree Application Checklist before submitting.

Step 5: Submit the Application to Enrol

Applications are submitted through the University’s MyWaikato Application Portal.

Candidates upload the required academic and supporting documents, provide evidence of their supervisor’s Invitation to Apply and enter their referees’ contact details.

Doctoral admission applications are normally considered monthly between February and November.

The University’s School or Faculty reviews each complete application before it proceeds through the institutional approval process.

Step 6: Apply for the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship

Scholarship applications are linked to the doctoral enrolment process.

The scholarship cannot be applied for as an entirely separate standalone opportunity.

The regulations state that applications are submitted as part of the application to enrol in a doctoral programme.

When applying through MyWaikato, candidates can provide additional information specifically supporting their scholarship case.

What You Need to Include in the Scholarship Application

The 2026 application asks candidates to provide several research-focused statements.

Proposed Thesis Information

Applicants must confirm:

  • Their proposed thesis title
  • Their approved Chief Supervisor

Academic and Research Preparation

Candidates must explain how their academic background, research experience and relevant professional experience have prepared them to undertake the proposed doctoral project.

Applicants are encouraged to provide specific examples rather than broad claims.

Contribution of the Research

Applicants must describe how the project will:

  • Advance knowledge, or
  • Influence practice in the relevant field

They should explain why the proposed contribution is timely and significant.

The University encourages applicants to identify the knowledge gap or problem their research addresses.

Mātauranga Māori, Pacific Knowledges and Te Tiriti o Waitangi

Applicants are asked to explain whether their research connects with:

  • Mātauranga Māori
  • Pacific knowledges
  • Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles and values

Where research involves Māori or Pacific communities or data, applicants should describe appropriate engagement and data-governance practices.

Broader Research Impact

Candidates are also asked to reflect on the significance of their proposed research beyond academia.

Potential impact can include contributions to:

  • Society
  • Economy
  • Environment
  • Health
  • Culture

Applicants should also discuss how they plan to engage with audiences that could use or benefit from the research.

Career Aspirations

Applicants must describe their career goals and explain how the doctoral research will help them achieve those goals.

They should also identify skills and capabilities they hope to develop through doctoral study.

References

Scholarship applicants may submit up to two references.

The scholarship application requires:

One academic reference, mandatory

This would normally come from someone familiar with the applicant’s previous academic study or research, often at the institution where the qualifying degree was completed.

Applicants may additionally submit:

One professional reference, optional

The professional referee should ideally be familiar with employment or experience relevant to the proposed doctoral research.

Scholarship Deadlines

Applications are considered during four rounds each year.

The official deadlines are:

  • 31 January
  • 30 April
  • 31 July
  • 31 October

Since the current date is August 2026, the next available scholarship application deadline is 31 October 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the deadline to begin the process because they need to:

  1. Identify an appropriate research supervisor
  2. Contact the supervisor
  3. Secure agreement to supervision
  4. Obtain an Invitation to Apply
  5. Prepare documentation
  6. Submit the doctoral Application to Enrol
  7. Receive an Offer of Place
  8. Complete the scholarship application

An Offer of Place must be received by the closing date of the relevant scholarship round.

When Will Applicants Receive a Decision?

Successful applicants are generally notified of their scholarship outcome within:

Up to eight weeks after the relevant application deadline.

Once offered the scholarship, recipients must accept it within 28 days, otherwise the offer lapses.

Full-Time Study Expectations

Recipients are normally expected to study full time.

Full-time scholarship holders should undertake approximately:

37.5 hours of doctoral study per week

They may take up to four weeks of annual holiday, excluding University and public holidays, without formally suspending the scholarship.

Can Scholarship Holders Work?

Yes, but employment restrictions apply.

Full-time scholarship holders are normally limited to:

500 hours of paid employment per year.

Applicants wanting to exceed this limit must obtain approval from the Scholarships Executive, and approval is generally reserved for exceptional circumstances.

This arrangement is intended to ensure that doctoral research remains the recipient’s principal commitment.

Part-Time Scholarship Arrangements

Part-time scholarship tenure may be permitted where students have compelling personal circumstances such as:

  • Illness
  • Disability
  • Parenting responsibilities
  • Caring responsibilities

Requests are considered individually.

During approved part-time study, the scholarship amount, tenure and employment allowances are adjusted proportionally.

Part-time status is not intended to allow recipients to undertake full-time employment while holding the doctoral scholarship.

Can You Hold Another Scholarship at the Same Time?

Certain smaller awards for research or conference purposes may be held alongside the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship.

Generally, lower-value awards may be held where the combined value of other awards does not exceed 50% of the doctoral scholarship’s annual living allowance.

Additional approval may be required where other funding exceeds this threshold.

Recipients offered a scholarship from a government sponsoring body or University partner, such as a China Scholarship Council scholarship, would normally need to relinquish the University-funded scholarship unless permission for concurrent tenure is granted.

Applicants should identify a research topic that fits both their academic background and the expertise available among University of Waikato supervisors.

Why Consider the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship?

For prospective research students, the University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship combines three important forms of support:

  • A substantial annual stipend
  • Doctoral tuition support
  • Structured institutional research supervision

The scholarship also places substantial weight on research impact, not merely grades.

Candidates are encouraged to show how their research could make a difference academically and beyond the University, whether through social, environmental, economic, cultural or health outcomes.

This makes the scholarship particularly relevant to applicants capable of articulating not only what they intend to research, but why the research matters.

Conclusion

The University of Waikato Doctoral Scholarship 2026 is an attractive funding opportunity for high-achieving domestic and international candidates seeking advanced research training in New Zealand.

The standard scholarship provides NZ$33,000 per year for up to 36 months, together with domestic doctoral tuition fees and the Student Services Fee.

Applicants must normally demonstrate at least an A- GPA, strong independent research potential and a well-developed doctoral project. They must also secure an appropriate University of Waikato supervisor, receive an Invitation to Apply, submit a complete doctoral application and obtain an Offer of Place before the relevant scholarship round closes.

Four application rounds are held each year, closing on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July and 31 October. For candidates applying after July 2026, the next deadline is 31 October 2026.

Because securing a supervisor and doctoral Offer of Place can take considerable time, prospective candidates should begin the process well before the scholarship deadline.
